title: Planck's Radiation Formula
short_intro: Planck's radiation law describes the spectral energy density of electromagnetic radiation emitted by a black body in thermal equilibrium at a definite temperature. It successfully resolves the ultraviolet catastrophe by introducing the quantum hypothesis of energy emission and absorption.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic understanding of black body radiation, statement of Planck's formula, limiting cases yielding Rayleigh-Jeans law and Wien's displacement law, and Stefan-Boltzmann law.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed derivation of Planck's formula using photon gas statistics or density of states in a cavity, frequency and wavelength distribution functions, and derivation of Wien's displacement constant.

concept_notes.heading: Black Body Cavity and Standing Waves
bullets: A black body cavity (Hohlraum) maintains thermal equilibrium through continuous absorption and emission of radiation by the walls.
Radiation inside the cavity forms standing electromagnetic waves satisfying boundary conditions at the walls.
The number of independent modes of vibration per unit volume in the frequency range ν to ν + dν is given by g(ν)dν = (8πν²/c³)dν.

concept_notes.heading: Planck's Quantum Hypothesis
bullets: Electromagnetic energy is not emitted or absorbed continuously, but in discrete packets called quanta or photons.
The energy of each oscillator or quantum is restricted to discrete values given by E = hν, where h is Planck's constant.
Average energy of an oscillator at absolute temperature T is determined using Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics as <E> = hν / (exp(hν/kT) - 1).

concept_notes.heading: Wien's Distribution Law as a Limit
bullets: At very high frequencies or low temperatures where hν >> kT, the exponential term exp(hν/kT) >> 1.
Planck's formula reduces to Wien's radiation formula: U(ν)dν = (8πhν³/c³) exp(-hν/kT) dν.
Wien's law accurately predicts spectral radiance in the short-wavelength (ultraviolet) region.

concept_notes.heading: Rayleigh-Jeans Law as a Limit
bullets: At very low frequencies or high temperatures where hν << kT, the exponential term can be expanded as exp(hν/kT) ≈ 1 + hν/kT.
Planck's formula reduces to the classical Rayleigh-Jeans law: U(ν)dν = (8πν²kT/c³)dν.
The Rayleigh-Jeans law fails at high frequencies, predicting infinite energy density, known as the ultraviolet catastrophe.

derivations.title: Wavelength Form of Planck's Law
derivations.conditions: Transformation of spectral energy density from frequency domain to wavelength domain using \nu = c/lambda
steps: Express frequency in terms of wavelength: \nu = \frac{c}{lambda}, hence d\nu = -\frac{c}{lambda^2} dlambda (ignoring negative sign for magnitude).
Substitute ν and dν into the frequency distribution formula U(ν)dν.
Simplify the resulting expression by collecting powers of λ and c.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Black Body Spectral Radiance Curves
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Curves of spectral energy density U(λ) versus wavelength λ for different absolute temperatures T, showing a distinct peak shifting toward shorter wavelengths as temperature increases.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Each curve peaks at a specific wavelength λmax governed by Wien's displacement law. The area under each curve increases steeply with temperature (T&sup4;). At long wavelengths, all curves converge, matching the Rayleigh-Jeans prediction.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in conceptual questions regarding the shift of peak wavelength with temperature and the failure of classical physics at short wavelengths.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Comparison of Planck's Law with Classical Laws
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of U(λ) vs λ showing experimental data points fitting Planck's curve perfectly, while the Rayleigh-Jeans curve diverges to infinity as λ approaches zero.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the ultraviolet catastrophe resolved by Planck's quantum assumption, proving classical equipartition fails for high-frequency modes.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via MCQ matching where students identify why Rayleigh-Jeans law fails at short wavelengths.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Fery's Black Body Furnace
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic diagram of a double-walled hollow spherical enclosure with a conical projection opposite to the aperture and a small pinhole.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Radiation entering the pinhole undergoes multiple internal reflections with negligible chance of escaping, making it an almost perfect black body absorber.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Standard apparatus question in viva voce and descriptive exam sections for experimental realization of black bodies.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the energy of a photon of frequency 5 × 10¹&sup4; Hz. (Given h = 6.63 × 10&sup-3;&sup4; J s)
solution_steps: Use Planck's energy relation: E = h\nu.
Substitute the given values: E = (6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}) \times (5 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}).

solved_numericals.question: Using Wien's displacement law, find the temperature of a stellar surface if its maximum spectral emission occurs at wavelength λmax = 500 nm. (Take b = 2.898 × 10&sup-3; m K)
solution_steps: State Wien's displacement law: lambda_{max} T = b.
Rearrange to solve for temperature: T = \frac{b}{lambda_{max}}.
Substitute values: T = \frac{2.898 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m K}}{500 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}}.

solved_numericals.question: At what wavelength does the spectral energy density of a black body reach its maximum at temperature T = 3000 K? (b = 2.898 × 10&sup-3; m K)
solution_steps: Apply Wien's displacement law formula: lambda_{max} = \frac{b}{T}.
Substitute the given temperature: lambda_{max} = \frac{2.898 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m K}}{3000 \text{ K}}.
Compute the wavelength: lambda_{max} = 9.66 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m} = 966 \text{ nm}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: Radiation inside the cavity consists of standing electromagnetic waves interacting with atomic oscillators whose energies are quantized as E = nhν. Limitation: The derivation assumes thermal equilibrium and ideal cavity walls, which is an idealized model approximated by practical black bodies.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Planck's formula predicts infinite energy at high frequencies.
common_misconceptions.correct: Planck's formula drops exponentially to zero at high frequencies.
common_misconceptions.why: The denominator factor exp(hν/kT) - 1 grows exponentially as frequency increases, suppressing high-frequency emission and avoiding the ultraviolet catastrophe.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Wien's law is valid for all wavelengths.
common_misconceptions.correct: Wien's law is only a valid approximation at short wavelengths (high frequencies).
common_misconceptions.why: At long wavelengths, the exponential term can no longer dominate, causing Wien's law to deviate significantly from experimental observations.

quick_revision: Planck's radiation law unifies Wien's law and Rayleigh-Jeans law through the quantum hypothesis E = hν.
